name: Bianca Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at half five, out to the ewes before the kids are awake. Luc and I rent eighty hectares from the county council, so it's sheep, thirty suckler cows, some spring barley and a field of turnips for winter feed. Most of the day is fixing what broke yesterday: a water trough, a gate, the old Ford tractor that only starts if you talk nicely to it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like lambing, even the nights, because you can see what you did with your own hands. What wears me out is the paperwork and the money. Luc drives the school bus mornings and afternoons, and that wage is what actually pays the mortgage on our cottage on Mill Lane, not the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so. Every year some salesman at the agricultural show tells me a computer is going to run my farm, and every year I still have to pull a lamb out by the legs at three in the morning. I'd probably say it a bit louder than that at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes, and nothing changing isn't great either. We're still behind on the rent review, the feed bill still goes up, and Maya still needs new school shoes. AI was never my problem, money was.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always. Get the ewes scanned in January, sell the store lambs in August, and hope the barley price holds. Maybe I'd finally get round to fixing the shed roof if we had a good autumn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. A bit tired, because relief doesn't pay the feed merchant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said money was the problem, not AI. Where does the money pressure bite hardest right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Feed and diesel. Last winter we bought in silage from Dennis down the road because ours got wet, and that was nearly two thousand we didn't have. We put it on the merchant's account and we're still paying it off at fifty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in the routine tasks AI might take that you'd actually be glad to lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The movement forms for the sheep, maybe, if someone else built it and it worked first time. I'm not going to go looking for it. Luc's sister does that kind of thing on her phone and it just looks like more things to go wrong.

S0.say: AI being mostly hype is what I always expected, because no computer has ever lambed a ewe for me. I'd say it plainly, and a bit louder at the pub.
S0.think: Nothing changing isn't good news either, because the farm was already struggling before anyone mentioned AI. Money, rent and feed costs are her real problem, not technology.
S0.do: Keeps the same calendar: scanning ewes in January, selling store lambs in August and paying off the feed merchant at fifty a week. Puts off the shed roof unless the autumn is good.
S0.feel: Relieved, but tired, because relief doesn't settle any bills.
S0.quote: AI was never my problem, money was.
S0.fieldNote: She treats this scenario as a return to her normal struggle rather than a good outcome. The weekly repayment on bought-in silage came up unprompted and says more about her than any view on technology. She brushes off even the useful bits of AI as one more thing to break.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farmers need a union that actually fights, because this is when the big operators grab the rest of the land. Gresham Farms over the hill already has robot milkers and a self-driving sprayer. I'd say the council should be protecting small tenants like us, not selling off holdings when people retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we're the ones who get squeezed out. If Gresham can do lambs and barley cheaper with machines, the price drops and our margin, which is already about nothing, goes below nothing. I don't have the money to buy those machines and I wouldn't know how to run them anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the farmers' union meeting in town, which I haven't done in years, and push them to fight for tenant farmers. At home we'd cut back: no holiday, no new quad bike, keep the old Ford going another five years. And I'd wait and see what the price of lamb does before I panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Like when the vet looks at a sick cow and doesn't say anything for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait before you panic. What would make you panic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the council wrote to say they were reviewing our tenancy because a bigger farm wanted to merge holdings. That letter would do it. We've seen it happen to the Pryce family two farms over, and they're in a flat in town now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any new job in this picture you could see yourself doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People keep saying 'robot technician'. I'm forty-three with a certificate in sheep and crops, I'm not going to be fixing computers. Maybe I'd do relief shepherding for other farms, if there's still any sheep left to shepherd.

S1.say: Small farmers need a union that fights back, because this is when big operators like Gresham Farms grab more land. The council should protect tenants instead of selling off holdings.
S1.think: She expects to be squeezed out, because machines on big farms will push down lamb and barley prices below her thin margin. She can't afford the machines and doesn't want to learn them.
S1.do: Goes back to farmers' union meetings to push for tenant protections. Cuts the holiday and the new quad bike, and keeps the old tractor going while watching lamb prices.
S1.feel: Tight in the chest, like waiting for bad news from the vet.
S1.quote: Like when the vet looks at a sick cow and doesn't say anything for a while.
S1.fieldNote: Her politics come straight out: big operators and a council that doesn't protect tenants are the villains. The Pryce family's eviction is her reference point for what failure looks like. She dismisses retraining quickly, which fits how much she avoids new technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be angry and I wouldn't hide it. I'd be posting on the union page that the government let tech companies run us over without a single plan. I'd say they need to stop it, or tax it until the people it throws out can eat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd lose the tenancy within a year. If a robot can do everything I do, the council will rent the land to whoever brings robots, and that's not us. Two years is no time at all, we can barely plan two seasons ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, we'd stop every bit of spending that isn't food or the mortgage, and Luc would ask for more hours on the buses while there are still bus drivers. I'd get to every meeting and protest the union ran. And I'd be at the council office asking what help there is for tenants before the queue gets long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Honestly, picturing it, I feel sick. Like I'm standing in the yard and the ground's gone soft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Maya and Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we might have to move and it's not their fault and it's not our fault either. Tom would ask about the dog. Maya would ask if she can still go to the same school, and I wouldn't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farm rent, because the council is slow and there's a process. The mortgage on the cottage comes first, always. After that the feed merchant, and I'd hate that, because the man who runs it has given us credit for twelve years.

S2.say: She would be openly angry that the government let tech companies run over farmers with no plan. She'd demand they stop it or tax it hard enough to feed the people it throws out.
S2.think: She privately expects to lose the tenancy within a year, because the council would rent the land to whoever brings robots. Two years is shorter than her usual planning horizon.
S2.do: Stops all spending except food and the mortgage, while Luc asks for extra bus hours. Goes to every union meeting and protest, and asks the council what help exists for tenants before the queue builds.
S2.feel: Sick, as if the ground in the yard has gone soft.
S2.quote: Two years is no time at all, we can barely plan two seasons ahead.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year timeline overwhelms her: there is no plan she can make that fits inside it. She puts the mortgage before the farm rent without hesitating, which shows the house matters more to her than the land. Her loyalty to the feed merchant is a small detail that says a lot about how she sees her community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same thing as the fast one but with more time to shout about it. I'd be telling everyone at the livestock market: we've got five years, so make the government write the rules now. A tax on farm robots, money for tenant farmers, something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two, but not by enough for someone like me. I'm not going to turn into a different person in five years. What it gives me is time to fight, and time to get the kids through school before it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union properly and go to the regional meetings, maybe stand for something. I'd write to our member of parliament about tenant protections, which I've never done. We'd cut back hard and try to clear the feed merchant debt by the second year, so at least we're not owing anyone when it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared but with something to do. That's better than just scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes with five years compared to two, in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two I'd just be grabbing whatever help there is. With five I can actually organise. There's maybe forty tenant farms on the council estate, and if we all said the same thing at once they'd have to listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you wouldn't learn the new machines. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe if someone sat next to me and showed me, and it wasn't on my own time and money. But I'm being honest: I'd rather spend those five years fighting for a fair deal than learning to babysit a robot that's taking my job.

S3.say: She'd tell everyone at the livestock market that five years is the time to make the government write rules now. She'd call for a tax on farm robots and money for tenant farmers.
S3.think: Five years is better than two, but not enough for her to become a different person. It mainly buys time to fight and to get the children through school before the change lands.
S3.do: Joins the union properly, goes to regional meetings and writes to the local member of parliament about tenant protections. Cuts back hard to clear the feed merchant debt by the second year.
S3.feel: Scared, but with something to do, which she says is better than just scared.
S3.quote: I'd rather spend those five years fighting for a fair deal than learning to babysit a robot that's taking my job.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time turns her panic into organising rather than adapting. She does the maths on the council estate's forty tenant farms herself, which shows she thinks in groups. She admits openly that she'd choose politics over retraining, and doesn't pretend otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for governments to do this properly, so there's no excuse. Land should go to communities and co-ops, not to whoever owns the most robots. I'd say that online and I'd say it at the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, in ten years I'd be fifty-three and Maya would be twenty-one. I think the farm would go in the end, but maybe I'd have got the kids out the other side first. That's what I'd measure it by, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still fight, but I'd also think about the kids' plans. We'd push Maya towards college and not the farm, which hurts to say. I'd keep the union work going and campaign for a land co-op on the council estate, so if robots come they're ours, not Gresham's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad more than scared. Like watching the last good weather of the year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd want the robots to be 'ours'. Wouldn't that mean learning them after all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You caught me. If it was a co-op, someone else in the co-op could run them, someone younger who likes that stuff. I'd do the stock and the hands-on bits for as long as there are any. That's not learning, that's sharing out the jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Maya if she wanted to farm anyway?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her not to rent, never rent, and to get the education I didn't. My own mum told me farming was a hard life and I didn't listen either. I'd probably cry and then help her.

S4.say: Ten years is enough time for governments to do this properly, so there is no excuse. Land should go to communities and co-ops rather than whoever owns the most robots.
S4.think: She thinks the farm would probably go in the end, but ten years might get her children safely through. She measures success by how the kids come out, not by whether she keeps farming.
S4.do: Keeps up union work and campaigns for a land co-op on the council estate so the robots belong to local tenants. Steers her daughter Maya towards college rather than the farm.
S4.feel: Sad more than scared, like the last good weather of the year.
S4.quote: I'd tell her not to rent, never rent, and to get the education I didn't.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, her focus shifts from her own job to her children's future. She handles the contradiction about learning robots by dividing the work inside a co-op, which is a neat way of keeping her values without changing her habits. She still expects to lose the farm, so her mood stays high even with time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, by 2028, no question. What would help is a guarantee that tenants can't be thrown off for a robot, and some money for families while they work out what's next. Not a course on a computer, money and a roof.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals. Everyone talks about jobs, but if it's all robots, who notices the ewe that's off her food before she's properly sick? Maybe the robot does. I'd still want to be the one who notices.

headlineQuote: I'd still want to be the one who notices.
portrait: Bianca Moreau is 43 and rents eighty hectares from the county council with her partner Luc, running sheep, suckler cows and barley, while his school bus wage pays the mortgage on their cottage. She is left-leaning, distrusts big operators like the neighbouring Gresham Farms, and avoids new technology. In the mild scenario she shrugs off AI because money was always her real problem. In the AGI scenarios she moves from panic about losing the tenancy within two years to organising tenant farmers and steering her daughter away from farming if there is a decade to prepare.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she expects to lose the council tenancy within a year with no time to plan.
whatWouldHelp: A guarantee that tenants can't be thrown off the land for a robot, and money for families while they work out what's next.
